[[File:BlackburnRovers FA Cup 1883-84.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.3|The [[Blackburn Rovers F.C.|Blackburn Rovers]] team which won the FA Cup in 1884. Team captain [[James Brown (footballer born 1862)|James Brown]] (front row, centre) holds the trophy.|alt=A group of men, most of whom are wearing shorts and football shirts, holding two trophies, one of which is the FA Cup]]
The Football Association Challenge Cup, commonly known as the [[FA Cup]], is a [[Single-elimination tournament|knockout]] competition in English [[Association football|football]], organised by and named after [[The Football Association]] (the FA), the governing body of the sport in England. It is the oldest existing football competition in the world,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2009/SPORT/football/05/28/oldest.cup.competitions/index.html|publisher=[[CNN]]|title=FA Cup final retains its global appeal|access-date=19 April 2026|first=Mike|last=Steere}}</ref> having commenced in the [[1871–72 FA Cup|1871–72 season]].<ref name="RS" /> The tournament is open to all clubs in the top 10 levels of the [[English football league system]], although a club's home stadium must meet certain requirements prior to entering the tournament.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thefa.com/TheFACup/CompetitionAdministration|publisher=The Football Association|title=FA Competition Administration|access-date=13 October 2010|archive-date=23 December 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111223215408/http://www.thefa.com/TheFACup/CompetitionAdministration|url-status=live}}</ref> The competition culminates at the end of the league season (usually in May) with the [[FA Cup final]], officially named The Football Association Challenge Cup Final Tie, which has traditionally been regarded as the showpiece finale of the English football season.<ref>{{cite news|work=The Independent|title=Football: FA Cup Final: Calamity for James as Di Matteo makes history|date=21 May 2000|first=Nick|last=Townsend }}</ref>

The vast majority of FA Cup final matches have been in London: most of these were played at the original [[Wembley Stadium (1923)|Wembley Stadium]], which was used from 1923 until the stadium closed in 2000. The other venues used for the final before 1923 were [[The Oval|Kennington Oval]], [[Crystal Palace National Sports Centre#FA Cup Finals (1895–1914)|Crystal Palace]], [[Stamford Bridge (stadium)|Stamford Bridge]] and [[Lillie Bridge Grounds|Lillie Bridge]], all in London, [[Goodison Park]] in Liverpool and [[Fallowfield Stadium]] and [[Old Trafford]] in Manchester. The [[Millennium Stadium]] in [[Cardiff]] hosted the final for six years (2001–2006), while the new Wembley Stadium was under construction. Other grounds have been used for replays, which until 1999 took place if the initial match ended in a draw. The [[Wembley Stadium|new Wembley Stadium]] has been the permanent venue of the final since 2007.

As of 2026, 45 clubs have won the FA Cup. The record for the most wins is held by [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]], with 14 victories.<ref name="RS" /> Only one surviving club, [[Blackburn Rovers F.C.|Blackburn Rovers]], have won the cup in three consecutive years, a feat that was also achieved by the now dissolved [[Wanderers F.C.|Wanderers]]; [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] are the only team to have lost three consecutive FA Cup finals. The cup has been won by the same team in two or more consecutive years on ten occasions, and four teams have won consecutive finals more than once: Wanderers, [[Blackburn Rovers F.C.|Blackburn Rovers]], [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]] and Arsenal.<ref name="RS" /> The cup has been won by a non-English team once: [[Cardiff City F.C.|Cardiff City]] in [[1927 FA Cup final|1927]]. The current holders are [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]], who defeated Chelsea in the [[2026 FA Cup final|2026 final]] for their eighth win, having become the first team to qualify for four consecutive FA Cup finals.

==History==
{{further|History of the FA Cup}}
[[Image:ArthurGrimsdell.jpg|thumb|upright=0.9|[[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]] captain [[Arthur Grimsdell]] displays the cup to fans on the Tottenham High Road after Spurs' victory in the 1921 final, the first win by a [[London]]-based team since the same club's win 20&nbsp;years earlier.|alt=An elderly man holding the FA Cup]]
The winners of [[1871–72 FA Cup|the first tournament]] were [[Wanderers F.C.|Wanderers]], a team of former [[Public school (United Kingdom)|public schoolboys]] based in [[London]], who went on to win the competition five times in its first seven seasons. The early winners of the competition were all teams of wealthy amateurs from the south of England,<ref name="S1">{{Cite book|last1=Soar|first1=Phil|first2=Martin|last2=Tyler|title=Encyclopedia of British Football|year=1983|publisher=Willow Books|isbn=0-00-218049-9|page=19}}</ref> but in [[1883 FA Cup final|1883]], [[Blackburn Olympic F.C.|Blackburn Olympic]] became the first team from the north to win the cup, defeating [[Old Etonians F.C.|Old Etonians]]. Upon his team's return to [[Blackburn]], Olympic captain [[Albert Warburton]] proclaimed: "The Cup is very welcome to [[Lancashire]]. It'll have a good home and it'll never go back to London".<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Soar|first1=Phil|first2=Martin|last2=Tyler|title=Encyclopedia of British Football|page=20}}</ref>
 
With the advent of [[professionalism]] at around the same time, the amateur teams quickly faded from prominence in the competition.<ref name="S1" /> The leading professional clubs formed [[The Football League]] in 1888.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Soar|first1=Phil|first2=Martin|last2=Tyler|title=Encyclopedia of British Football|pages=16–17}}</ref> Since then, one [[Non-league football|non-league]] team has won the cup. [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]], then of the [[Southern Football League|Southern League]], defeated [[Sheffield United F.C.|Sheffield United]] of The Football League to win the [[1901 FA Cup final|1901 final]].<ref name="tele">{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/2288010/FA-Cup-by-numbers.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/2288010/FA-Cup-by-numbers.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=FA Cup by numbers|first=Christopher |last=Lyles|work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|access-date=24 October 2008|date=5 January 2008}}{{cbignore}}</ref> A year later Sheffield United returned to the final and won the cup, which then remained in the hands of [[Northern England|Northern]] and [[The Midlands|Midland]] clubs until Tottenham won it again in [[1921 FA Cup final|1921]].<ref name="RS" /> In [[1927 FA Cup final|1927]], [[Cardiff City F.C.|Cardiff City]], a team which plays in the [[English football league system]] despite being based in [[Wales]], won the cup, the only non-English club to do so.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/7328650.stm|title=Cardiff in footsteps of FA Cup giants|first=Peter|last=Shuttleworth|publisher=BBC Sport|access-date=24 October 2008|date=9 May 2008|archive-date=1 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170901205505/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/7328650.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Scotland|Scottish]] club [[Queen's Park F.C.|Queen's Park]] reached the final twice in the early years of the competition.<ref name="RS" />

The competition was not held during the [[First World War|First]] and [[Second World War|Second]] World Wars, except in the [[1914–15 in English football|1914–15 season]], when it was completed, and the [[1939–40 in English football|1939–40 season]], when it was abandoned during the qualifying rounds.<ref name="RS" />

[[Newcastle United F.C.|Newcastle United]] enjoyed a brief spell of FA Cup dominance in the 1950s, winning the trophy three times in five years,<ref name="RS" /> and in the 1960s, [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]] enjoyed a similar spell of success, with three wins in seven seasons. This marked the start of a successful period for London-based clubs, with 11&nbsp;wins in 22&nbsp;seasons.<ref name="S27">{{Cite book|last1=Soar|first1=Phil|first2=Martin|last2=Tyler|title=Encyclopedia of British Football|pages=27}}</ref> Teams from the second tier of English football, at the time called the [[Football League Second Division|Second Division]], experienced an unprecedented run of cup success between 1973 and 1980.<ref name="S27" /> [[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland]] won the cup in [[1973 FA Cup final|1973]], [[Southampton F.C.|Southampton]] repeated the feat in [[1976 FA Cup final|1976]], and [[West Ham United F.C.|West Ham United]] won in [[1980 FA Cup final|1980]], the most recent victory by a team from outside the top division.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="tele" />

Until 1999, a draw in the final would result in the match being replayed at a later date;<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/fa_cup/4235997.stm|title=FA Cup in danger of losing lustre|publisher=BBC Sport|first=Phil|last=McNulty|access-date=24 October 2008|date=4 February 2005|archive-date=8 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200608175415/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/fa_cup/4235997.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> since then the final has always been decided on the day, with a [[Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] as required.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.thefa.com/TheFACup/FACompetitions/TheFACup/Rules|title=Rules of The FA Challenge Cup|publisher=The Football Association|access-date=13 October 2010|archive-date=23 January 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230123190525/https://www.thefa.com/TheFACup/FACompetitions/TheFACup/Rules|url-status=live}}</ref> As of 2022 a penalty shoot-out has been required on only three occasions, in the 2005, 2006 and 2022 finals. [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] hold the record for the highest number of FA Cup wins, having claimed the trophy 14 times, most recently in 2020.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/53546100|title=FA Cup final 2020: Arsenal 2–1 Chelsea|publisher=BBC Sport|access-date=6 August 2020|date=1 August 2020|archive-date=1 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801202716/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/53546100|url-status=live}}</ref>
